cards.front: Who qualifies as a 'specified adult' under FINRA's senior exploitation rules?
cards.back: (1) Any individual age 65 or older, OR (2) any individual age 18 or older whom the member reasonably believes has a mental or physical impairment that renders the person unable to protect their own interests.

cards.front: Financial exploitation (FINRA definition)
cards.back: The wrongful or unauthorized taking, withholding, appropriation, or use of a specified adult's funds or securities; OR any act/omission to obtain control—through deception, intimidation, or undue influence—over the specified adult's money, assets, or property (including via power of attorney or guardianship).

cards.front: When must a member firm make reasonable efforts to obtain the name and contact info of a trusted contact person?
cards.back: When opening a customer's account or when updating account information for an existing account.

cards.front: Can a member firm open an account if the customer refuses to provide a trusted contact person?
cards.back: Yes. The firm only needs to make a reasonable effort to obtain the information (e.g., asking the customer). Refusal does not prohibit opening the account.

cards.front: What is the maximum length of a temporary hold on disbursements under FINRA's senior exploitation rule?
cards.back: Up to 15 business days. A state regulator or court may terminate it sooner or extend it longer.

cards.front: When a member firm places a temporary hold on disbursements due to suspected exploitation, when must it notify the trusted contact person and authorized parties?
cards.back: No later than two business days after the date the hold was initiated. (Notification is not required if the trusted contact is unavailable or is reasonably believed to be the perpetrator.)

cards.front: When a firm places a temporary hold on a senior's account, what internal action is required?
cards.back: The firm must immediately begin an internal review of the facts and circumstances that caused it to place the hold.

cards.front: Improper use of customer assets
cards.back: Any use of customer funds or securities in a way other than as intended by the customer. The most common example is borrowing from or lending to customers. All such improper uses are prohibited.

cards.front: List examples of 'red flags' that should alert a firm to potential improper use of customer assets.
cards.back: Suspicious transfers/disbursements in customer accounts; activity in a deceased person's account; excessive customer complaints; and exception reports showing discrepancies such as mismatched addresses, ZIP codes, or telephone area codes.

cards.front: What are the five permitted types of lending arrangements between a registered representative and a customer?
cards.back: (1) Immediate family relationship (no notice/approval needed); (2) Customer is in the business of lending money, e.g., a bank (no approval needed); (3) Both are registered persons at the same firm (firm approval required); (4) Personal relationship outside the broker-customer relationship (firm approval required); (5) Business relationship outside the broker-customer relationship (firm approval required).

cards.front: Seabird Securities has no written procedures permitting borrowing/lending between reps and customers. From which of the following could a rep borrow: (A) Uncle Joe, (B) college buddy Dustin, (C) optometrist Dr. DuVall, or (D) none?
cards.back: (D) Under no circumstance. If the firm has no procedures permitting such arrangements, the rep may not enter into any borrowing/lending arrangement with a customer—even from an immediate family member is moot here because the firm itself must allow it.

cards.front: May a BD, IA, or registered representative guarantee a customer against losses or guarantee a gain?
cards.back: No. All guarantees—or anything intended to convey a guarantee—against loss or of a gain are strictly prohibited.

cards.front: Under what conditions may a registered representative share in profits and losses in a customer's account?
cards.back: Only with prior written firm approval, a joint account must be established, and the rep may share only in proportion to their actual financial contribution (dollars contributed—not knowledge or expertise).

cards.front: What is the exception to the proportionate-sharing rule for joint accounts?
cards.back: When sharing a joint account with immediate family members, directly proportionate sharing is not required. Immediate family includes parents, in-laws, spouses, children, and anyone to whom the rep contributes financial support (broadly, anyone living in the same residence).

cards.front: May a firm share in a loss in a customer's account?
cards.back: Yes—only if the loss was due to an error made by the firm.

cards.front: May firms have joint accounts with customers?
cards.back: No. Firms are prohibited from having joint accounts with customers.

cards.front: What activities are nonregistered employees of a broker-dealer permitted to perform?
cards.back: Responding to general, non-investment questions (hours, taking messages, directions); providing literature on request; setting appointments; inviting prospects to seminars; and handling customer money and securities (if fingerprinted).

cards.front: What activities are nonregistered persons prohibited from performing?
cards.back: They may NOT engage in investment banking or securities business—including opening accounts, soliciting trades, giving recommendations, or discussing specific securities/investments with customers.

cards.front: Must nonregistered personnel be fingerprinted?
cards.back: Yes, if they handle customer funds or securities. Fingerprinting is required for those handling customer assets.

cards.front: After passing the SIE exam, are you a registered representative?
cards.back: No. You are not registered until you pass a qualifying top-off exam (e.g., Series 6, 7). Until then, you are limited to the activities permitted of a nonregistered person.

cards.front: A BD's receptionist opens all incoming mail and forwards it to various departments. Must the receptionist be fingerprinted? Must they be registered with FINRA?
cards.back: Must be fingerprinted (handles customer assets/mail that may include checks or securities) but need NOT be registered with FINRA.
